title: ETGS: Explicit Thermodynamics Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Thermal Reconstruction
claim: Our method matches the quality of slow dynamic baselines while rendering and training at speeds close to fast static methods.
layout: 7 panels in one row, left-to-right, speed/PSNR overlay captions on each panel
description: A single horizontal strip of seven rendered thermal images of the same scene, a bench-like frame seen in false-color infrared (blue background, cyan to green and orange where it is hotter). Each panel has a dark translucent caption bar at the bottom. The bars give the method name with fps, then training time and PSNR: 3DGS, Mip-Splatting, Thermal3D-GS, NTR-Gaussian, 4DGS, Ours, and Ground Truth. Static baselines are fast (584 and 606 fps) but have low PSNR (29–32) and miss the warm glow at the lower left. Slower dynamic methods reach about 35.6 PSNR but need 1000+ s of training. Ours reaches 38.25 PSNR, 458 fps and 185 s of training, and its render is the closest to the ground truth. The eye goes to the warm patch at the lower left and then to the numbers.
caption: Our method achieves high-quality rendering of dynamic thermal scenes with efficiency comparable to static methods (Kerbl et al. (2023); Yu et al. (2024)). The key to this performance is the novel explicit modeling of dynamic thermal Gaussians based on thermodynamics, which significantly speeds up scene optimization and synthesis of new views, while achieving state-of-the-art quality.
abstract: We propose ETGS, a method for reconstructing dynamic thermal scenes by embedding explicit thermodynamic modeling into 3D Gaussian Splatting. Each Gaussian is equipped with physically interpretable thermal parameters, and its thermodynamics evolution is described by a first-order heat-transfer ODE with an analytical closed-form solution. This formulation avoids numerical integration, enables efficient rendering at arbitrary timestamps, and naturally handles irregular sampling and out-of-order observations. We also introduce the Rapid Heat Dynamics (RHD) dataset, which provides millisecond-aligned RGB–IR image pairs covering typical thermal processes such as cooling, warming, heating, and heat transfer. Experiments on RHD show that ETGS captures rapid thermal dynamics more accurately than existing static and dynamic baselines, while maintaining training and rendering efficiency close to that of static 3DGS. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jankin-wang/ETGS.
